gloss: work, serve; servant; service (Aramaic: do, make)
summary: עָבַד is to work and to serve: to work the ground or a task, to serve a master as a bondman or a king as a subject, and to serve a god with worship and obedience, so that “whom you will serve” is the choice between Yahweh and other gods. עֶבֶד is the one who serves, from the bought slave to the king’s officer, the man who calls himself “your servant”, and Yahweh’s servants Moses, David, the prophets, Israel and the servant of Isaiah 42–53; עֲבֹדָה is the work or service itself, from Egypt’s hard bondage to the Levites’ service of the tent and the Passover rite. Scripture’s Aramaic uses עֲבַד for “do, make”, where Hebrew says עָשָׂה, and serves with פְּלַח; Hebrew itself sets עָבַד beside עָשָׂה (Isa 28:21). In Lev 23 the holy convocations forbid מְלֶאכֶת עֲבֹדָה, “work of service”, ordinary labour.

cognates.note: Six attestations, all Neo-Assyrian, the period when Aramaic was spoken across Assyria; it may be a borrowing from West Semitic rather than an inherited word. Named on עֶבֶד as possible only, so it counts neither way.

doctrine.statement: Israel served Egypt in hard bondage and groaned under it (Exo 1:13–14; 2:23). Yahweh’s demand to Pharaoh uses the same verb for the new master: “Let my son go, that he may serve me” (Exo 4:23; 7:16), and the sign to Moses was that the people would serve God at the mountain (Exo 3:12). So Israel are Yahweh’s servants because he brought them out of Egypt, and may not be sold as slaves (Lev 25:42, 55); Egypt is “the house of slaves” (Exo 20:2). The service is exclusive: “You shall fear Yahweh your God and serve him” (Deu 6:13), and not bow down to other gods nor serve them (Exo 20:5); Joshua sets the choice, “choose this day whom you will serve … as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh” (Jos 24:14–15). When Israel would not serve Yahweh with joy, they served their enemies (Deu 28:47–48), and Malachi’s day will show the difference between one who serves God and one who does not (Mal 3:18). Jesus answers the tempter with Deu 6:13, “him only shall you serve” (Mat 4:10), and says no one can serve two masters (Mat 6:24); Paul writes that a man is the servant of whom he obeys, whether of sin or of righteousness, and that those set free from sin have become servants of God (Rom 6:16–22); the Thessalonians turned from idols to serve the living and true God (1Th 1:9). From the verses: redemption is a change of masters, not the end of service; Yahweh frees his people from bondage to serve him, and service given to another is taken from him.

Yahweh calls Israel “my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen” (Isa 41:8), yet Israel is a blind servant (Isa 42:19). He also presents a servant whom he upholds, his chosen, on whom he puts his spirit, who will bring justice to the nations (Isa 42:1–4); Matthew says this was fulfilled in Jesus, quoting it in full (Mat 12:17–21), and the Peshitta has עַבְדָּא there. The servant restores Jacob and is a light to the nations (Isa 49:5–6), which Paul and Barnabas take as their own commission (Act 13:47). Yahweh’s servant will act wisely and be high and lifted up (Isa 52:13); he is despised, bears the sins of many, is led as a lamb to the slaughter, and by his knowledge the righteous servant makes many righteous and bears their iniquities (Isa 53:3–12). Philip begins from Isa 53:7–8 and preaches Jesus (Act 8:32–35); Peter quotes the chapter of Christ’s sufferings (1Pe 2:22–25); Jesus says “he was numbered with the transgressors” must be fulfilled in him (Luk 22:37); and Peter preaches that God “glorified his servant Jesus” (Act 3:13). Paul writes that Christ took the form of a servant, the Peshitta’s עַבְדָּא, humbled himself and became obedient to death, the death of the cross; therefore God highly exalted him (Php 2:7–9), the order of Isa 52:13–53:12. Jesus himself came not to be served but to serve and to give his life a ransom for many (Mrk 10:45). Moses was faithful in Yahweh’s house as a servant, Christ as a son over his house (Num 12:7; Heb 3:5–6). From the verses: the servant of Isaiah is Jesus, whose service is his obedience to death for the sins of many, and whose exaltation follows from it.

The Passover is called a עֲבֹדָה, a service Israel keeps in the land, and the children ask, “What do you mean by this service?” (Exo 12:25–27; 13:5). The Levites are given to Yahweh to serve the service of the tent, and the priesthood is “a service of gift” (Num 8:11; 18:6–7). Yahweh says he did not burden Israel with service in offerings, but they burdened him with service by their sins (Isa 43:23–24). Paul counts “the service” among Israel’s gifts (Rom 9:4), Hebrews describes the priests accomplishing the service of the first tent as a figure until the time of reformation (Heb 9:1, 6–10), and Christ’s blood cleanses the conscience from dead works “to serve the living God” (Heb 9:14). Paul calls believers to present their bodies a living sacrifice, “your reasonable service” (Rom 12:1). From the verses: the rites of the feasts were service rendered to Yahweh, pointing forward; the service he now asks is the whole life offered through Christ.

note: Root key עבד. Sounds: Arabic, Ugaritic and Sabaic all show ʿ behind ע for both “serve” and “servant”; no cognate shows ġ, so there is no split behind the merged letter. The Aramaic and Punic sense “do, make” has no cognate in a language that keeps ʿ and ġ apart (Arabic عبد does not mean “do”), so its older sound is not shown by evidence; it is kept as one root with the Hebrew, which itself pairs עָבַד with עָשָׂה (Isa 28:21). No cognate was found for “till, work the ground”; scripture’s own use (Gen 2:5, 15; Exo 20:9) carries that sense. BDB key notes: p.ac.aa also counts the names עוֹבֵד/עֹבֵד אֱדֹם (11 tokens, “(no stem)”) and one Aramaic token (Ezr 7:18, “Peal”); xp.aa.aa counts one Hebrew token (Exo 3:12, qal) by spelling. The four “hophal” tokens (Exo 20:5, 23:24, Deu 5:9, 13:3) are kept with the qal sense “serve other gods”. Left out: the names עֶבֶד מֶלֶךְ (p.ac.ag, whose 907 tokens are in fact מֶלֶךְ filed by spelling), עֹבֵד אֱדֹם, עֶבֶד (n.pr., p.ac.ac), עַבְדִּי, עֹבַדְיָהוּ, עוֹבֵד, עֲבֵד נְגוֹ (both keys), עַבְדּוֹן, עַבְדָּא, עַבְדְּאֵל, עַבְדִּיאֵל: names belong in names/. Cross-reference keys m.ct.af and xm.al.ag have no tokens. Peshitta words from SEDRA root 1328 (lexemes 2219–2226, 3544, 3514) with verses from the BFBS word list; not entered: lexeme 2219 ܡܥܒܕܢܐ “worker” (Rom 4:15 only, mentioned in the summary of מַעְבְּדָנוּתָא), 3544 ܡܫܥܒܕܐ “subjected” (2Ti 3:3, one token) and 3514 (one token, Heb 12:27, no gloss in SEDRA). Peshitta checks: Mat 12:18 and Php 2:7 use ܥܒܕܐ; Act 3:13, 26, Mat 6:24 do not (not ʿabdā), so those are cited only from the Greek. The Peshitta’s “serve” is mostly ܦܠܚ (SEDRA root ILK), as Biblical Aramaic serves with פְּלַח (Dan 3:28; 6:21). (2) Whether Act 3:13’s παῖς “servant” should be read as an allusion to Isa 52:13 (ἐδόξασεν; LXX δοξασθήσεται); the doctrine cites it only as Peter’s words. (3) The Greek λατρεία link to Rom 12:1 and Hebrews is through the Septuagint’s rendering of עֲבֹדָה (Exo 12:25–26), a bridge only. (4) The Syriac vocalisations in Hebrew script are standard forms, not copied from SEDRA’s vocalised words.
